prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are interrogated with fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, and for bringing many-atom quantum control to the measurement of time

statement.case_for: After reading the whole first round I keep optical lattice clocks as my single-part choice, and I hold it for scientific reasons, not because four of us ended up in the same place. The discovery content is a physics idea: at the magic wavelength the differential light shift of the clock transition cancels, so atoms can be held tightly and interrogated in large numbers without the trap spoiling the transition. Ye's group then showed what that buys: many-body effects (collisional and spin-orbit shifts, correlated ensembles) understood and controlled, and stability and systematic uncertainty near 1e-18. That is the kind of result I trust, because independent groups in Japan, the US, France, Germany and China reproduce it and clock-to-clock frequency-ratio comparisons agree at the level the claims need. Theory and experiment agree quantitatively on the shifts, which is my own field's standard. The credit is the cleanest on the shortlist: the same two names appeared in every opening proposal, and Katori's proposal and first strontium lattice demonstration and Ye's push to the 1e-18 regime are separable, documented contributions. My citation is built on the lattice concept and its realisation. It does not mention the redefinition of the second, because that is a consequence decided by metrologists and not a condition of the discovery.
statement.case_against: The honest weakness is novelty. Hall and Haensch (2005) gave us the comb and Wineland and Haroche (2012) gave us single-ion control and ion clocks, so a sceptic can read lattice clocks as the third instalment of one optical-metrology line, and I concede that this reading is not absurd. I also concede that Lemonde, Gill, Hollberg, Ludlow, Hinkley, Takamoto and the ion-clock groups produced decisive milestones that two names do not cover, and that the redefinition of the second has not happened. Finally, this is a precision-measurement prize and speaks less directly than twisted graphene to the question I personally find most striking, namely what new matter or new boundary we have uncovered. If the committee concludes that the comb and ion prizes already exhausted this territory, I would move to atom interferometry or to magic-angle graphene, but I do not yet think the evidence says that.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks lattice clocks seventh, suggests waiting for the SI redefinition, and prefers magic-angle graphene because it ties a simple, checkable mechanism to a decisive experiment.
responses.response: I accept the quality of the Bistritzer-MacDonald argument. A flat-band condition that can be checked on paper and then found in a device is exactly the sort of clean chain I admire. On the clock timing I stay where I was: the Nobel test is established and reproduced physics, and the 1e-18 comparisons satisfy it whether the CGPM acts in 2030 or later. Waiting would make the prize depend on a decision about a convention, not on the physics. Your chain also has a gap that mine lacks, since the experimental discovery names only one of the people who made it, and the mechanism behind the superconducting phase, the part that gives the field its excitement, is still open. My view of B015 has not changed: it is my second-tier alternative.

responses.point: Olsson argues that magic-angle graphene is the original experiment, a falsifiable prediction confirmed by a tunable platform, and treats the clock as the compact and defensible alternative.
responses.response: The original-experiment test is a fair one and B015 passes it better than the clock does, because Katori's idea and the first lattice demonstrations date to the early 2000s but the 1e-18 performance only emerged over the next decade. Where I come out differently is on what the three-name credit can carry. Jarillo-Herrero alone cannot stand for an experiment on which Yuan Cao was lead author, and the Dean group's work in parallel makes the experimental side harder to draw. My question to you is whether you would accept a citation that names only the flat-band prediction and the correlated insulators, with the pairing mechanism set aside, and still be comfortable with who is left out. That is the form I would need to see before moving B015 above the clock.

responses.point: Kroll asks that the citation name the magic-wavelength concept and the accuracy rather than the redefinition of the second, and that the clock not be described as a spin-off of the frequency comb.
responses.response: I agree on both and have rewritten my citation accordingly: it names the lattice clock, the magic-wavelength trapping and the 1e-18 uncertainty and leaves the SI second out. I also accept your separation of Katori's proposal and Ye's accuracy work from the follow-on milestones, which makes the two-name credit more defensible than I made it in round 1. Where we still differ is the wording about applications. I would not put geodesy or dark-matter searches in the citation, because they are uses and the discovery is the control of many atoms. I also still keep atom interferometry as an alternative and not as a partner part, because the Borde, Pritchard, Kasevich, Mueller and Chu allocation is not settled.

responses.point: Johansson moved from circuit QED to optical lattice clocks after reading all eight ballots, and shares the view that the citation should stay on the lattice concept and its 1e-18 realisation.
responses.response: I value that you moved on the evidence, and I want to be clear that I do not take your move or any count of rankings as an argument. The reason for the clock is the reproducibility record. Your caution about the 2005 and 2012 prizes is the one I weigh most, and I answer it this way: the comb is the ruler and ion control is a different platform, whereas the lattice with its magic wavelength is what allows an ensemble to be used, and the ion clocks cannot do this. Since you work closest to the quantum-technology side, I would like your view whether the many-atom, quantum-limited interrogation gives a distinct discovery or whether you read it as engineering. If distinct, I think the committee can say so plainly in the citation.

responses.point: Eriksson puts magic-angle graphene first as a case of theory and experiment closing the loop, and notes that eight members' support for B057 does not by itself outweigh attribution cleanliness against novelty.
responses.response: Your last point is the one I most agree with: breadth of ranking should not decide anything, and I am not relying on it. The weighing I would defend is attribution cleanliness together with a decade of cross-laboratory agreement against novelty. On novelty, I accept that the 2018 observation of correlated states at the predicted angle surprised many, and that it closes a loop more dramatically than a clock does. On maturity, though, I read eight years with the pairing mechanism unresolved, a trio that omits Cao and a priority question about Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto as a larger unforced risk than anything on the clock side. I would be glad to revisit if the committee decides the credit for B015 is tidier than I now think.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that lattice clocks are distinct from the 2005 comb and the 2012 ion-control prizes, which I judge the main risk to my position.
Whether leaving out Lemonde, Gill, Hollberg, Ludlow and the ion-clock groups will be seen as an unfair omission, or as the unavoidable boundary of a two-name prize.
I cannot independently verify the latest uncertainty figures for individual clocks or the date of the redefinition of the second.

If a colleague shows that the magic-angle graphene credit can be settled, my ranking of B015 against B057 could change, since my objection there is attribution and maturity and not doubt about the physics.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with Katori, Ye or their groups. I am a theoretical atomic physicist with a long-standing collaboration with Anne L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, and I have worked with Reinhold Schuch on Stockholm storage-ring recombination theory, but none of this touches lattice clocks, optical metrology or the credited names. The neighbouring AMO alternatives (B035, B005) lie close to my community, and I know of no tie to Bordé, Pritchard, Kasevich, Müller or the optical-lattice simulation groups. I disclose that proximity as a field, not as a conflict.
